g: To habitually go to (someone in distress, sickness etc.) to comfort them. (Now generally merged into later senses, below.)
To go and meet (a person) as an act of friendliness or sociability.
x: She decided to visit her grandparents for Christmas.

g: Of God: to appear to (someone) to comfort, bless, or chastise or punish them. (Now generally merged into later senses, below.)
x: [God] hath visited and redeemed his people.
Then she arose with her daughters in law, that she might return from the country of Moab: for she had heard in the country of Moab how that the Lord had visited his people in giving them bread.

g: To punish, to inflict harm upon (someone or something).
x: Her life was spared by the clemency of the emperor, but he visited the pomp and treasures of her palace.

g: Of a sickness, misfortune etc.: to afflict (someone).
x: There used to be a sharp contest as to where the effigy was to be made, for the people thought that the house from which it was carried forth would not be visited with death that year.

g: To inflict punishment, vengeance for (an offense) on or upon someone.
x: 05-032 was right about one thing: there is only one way to defeat the enemy, and that is to visit utter annihilation on it.
If this were an Ibsen play, we would be thinking of the sins of one generation being visited upon another, he said.

g: To go to (a shrine, temple etc.) for worship. (Now generally merged into later senses, below.)
To go to (a place) for pleasure, on an errand, etc.
x: Each year, millions of people visit the 4,570-meter-high Baishui Glacier in southern China.

g: A single act of visiting.
x: Next time you're in Manchester, give me a visit.
We paid a quick visit to James on the way up to Scotland.

There was some laughter, and Roddle was left free to expand his ideas on the periodic visits of cowboys to the town. “Mason Rickets, he had ten big punkins a-sittin' in front of his store, an' them fellers from the Upside-down-F ranch shot 'em up […].”

g: A meeting with a doctor at their surgery or the doctor's at one's home.
Someone who visits someone else; someone staying as a guest.
x: He ventured to raise his eyes again, and found his supernatural visitor confronting him in an erect attitude, with its chain wound over and about its arm.
"'Tis some visiter," I muttered, "tapping at my chamber door— / Only this, and nothing more."
The Riley Packaging plant in Uganda is quite a sight. From wall to wall and floor to ceiling, it is crammed with vast rolls of paper. A visitor feels like an ant gazing at stacks of toilet rolls.

g: Someone who pays a visit to a specific place or event; a sightseer or tourist.
x: Warwick observed, as they passed through the respectable quarter, that few people who met the girl greeted her, and that some others whom she passed at gates or doorways gave her no sign of recognition; from which he inferred that she was possibly a visitor in the town and not well acquainted.
Belgrade knew how to show visitors a good time, thanks to its fashionable, somewhat raucous nightclub and bar scene.

g: Someone, or a team, that is playing away from home.
x: But, somewhat against the run of play, Craddock fired the visitors ahead, volleying a low effort beyond Simon Mignolet after Sunderland twice failed to clear attempted crosses from Stephen Hunt.

g: A person authorized to visit an institution to see that it is being managed properly.
x: As to eleemoſynary corporations, by the dotation the founder and his heirs are of common right the legal viſitors, to ſee that that property is rightly employed, which would otherwiſe have deſcended to the viſitor himſelf: […]

g: An extraterrestrial being on Earth.
x: 5: Of course there is always the remote (I hope) possibility that instant panic will prompt us to send a hailstorm of nuclear warheads out upon the visitor.
The visitor in Man Facing South-east claims pure altruism; Rantes (Hugo Soto) wants to alleviate the suffering of the poor and helpless.
The tower radioed the flight leader, Captain Thomas F. Mantell, Jr., and requested that he engage and attempt to identify the strange visitor.

g: An object which lands or passes by Earth or its orbit.
x: Within a few months, another small meteoric mass has been added to the list of those extra-terrestrial bodies which have fallen within the limits of Tennessee. This recent visitor is a stone, weighing, when first obtained, three pounds.

Though Clube and Napier’s cometary visitor was not a planet, the story is surprisingly close to that of Worlds in Collision.

g: A head or overseer of an institution such as a college (in which case, equivalent to the university's chancellor) or cathedral or hospital, who resolves disputes, gives ceremonial speeches, etc.
The object in the visitor pattern that performs an operation on the elements of a structure one by one.

visor.etym: From Middle English viser, from Anglo-Norman viser and Old French visiere.

g: A part of a helmet, arranged so as to lift or open, and so show the face. The openings for seeing and breathing are generally in it.
x: A close helmet entirely covers the head, face, and neck, having on the front perforations for the admission of air, and slits through which the wearer may see objects around him, this part which is stiled the visor lifts up by means of a pivot over each ear.

g: A mask for the face.
x:
No visor does become black villainy
So well as soft and tender flattery.

g: The fore piece of a cap, projecting over, and protecting the eyes.
A rigid adjustable flap on an automobile windshield that can shield the eyes of a driver from direct sunlight or glare.
plural of visual art

vital.etym: From Middle English vital, from Old French vital, from Latin vītālis (“of life, life-giving”), from vīta (“life”), from vīvō (“to live”). Doublet of jiva and quick.

g: Relating to or characteristic of life.
x: vital energies; vital functions; vital actions

But open converse is there none,
⁠So much the vital spirits sink
⁠To see the vacant chair, and think,
‘How good! how kind! and he is gone.’

g: Necessary to the continuation of life; being the seat of life; being that on which life depends.
x: The brain is a vital organ.
And doen the heavens afford him vitall food?
We have argued that organizatory agents are operative in all vital processes, processes that overstep the limits of the physicochemical; […]

g: Invigorating or life-giving.
Necessary to continued existence.
x: The transition to farming was vital for the creation of civilisation.

g: Relating to the recording of life events.
x: Birth, marriage and death certificates are vital records.

g: Very important.
x: It is vital that you don't forget to do your homework.

David Cameron insists that his latest communications data bill is “vital to counter terrorism”. Yet terror is mayhem. It is no threat to freedom. That threat is from counter-terror, from ministers capitulating to securocrats.
Vocabulary is a vital component of educational success in both first and second language contexts.

g: Containing life; living.
x: spirits that live throughout, vital in every part
I ought to go upright and vital, and speak the rude truth in all ways.
The dart […]pierced a vital part.

g: Lively, having vitality
x: Montreal is a charming vital city with a large lesbian and gay population which clusters around a neighborhood not far from the center of town.

g: Capable of living; in a state to live; viable.
x: Pythagoras and Hippocrates […] affirming the birth of the seventh month to be vital.

g: Any of a specific group of organic compounds essential in small quantities for healthy human growth, metabolism, development, and body function. They are found in minute amounts in plant and animal foods or sometimes produced synthetically, and deficiencies of specific vitamins produce specific disorders.
x: a food rich in vitamins

g: preceding a word or its initial letter, to imply that the referent benefits health or wellness
x: Vitamin N: The Essential Guide to a Nature-Rich Life
I just follow three three Cs: clean living, chewing thoroughly, and a daily dose of vitamin Church

g: The patchy loss of skin pigmentation.
x: In the weeks that followed, I began to notice other people with vitiligo. On the streets, in the stores, in their cars. My God, they were everywhere!

g: Alphos, a form of leprosy.
Clear, detailed, or powerful.
Bright, intense, or colourful.
x: The half-dozen pieces […] were painted white and carved with festoons of flowers, birds and cupids. To display them the walls had been tinted a vivid blue which had now faded, but the carpet, which had evidently been stored and recently relaid, retained its original turquoise.

g: Full of life; strikingly alive.
x: The vivid, untrammeled life appealed to him, and for a time he had found delight in it; but he was wise and knew that once peace was established there would be no room in Cuba for the Sin Verguenza.

vizier.etym: From Ottoman Turkish وزیر (vezir) (Turkish vezir) (via French vizir), from Arabic وَزِير (wazīr, “helper, aide, minister”, literally “one who bears (the burden of office)”). Doublet of wazir.

g: A high-ranking official or minister in an Islamic government, especially in the Ottoman Empire.
The highest-ranking official or minister in ancient Egypt or Ebla; a chief administrator or a chancellor.
An ancient Mesopotamian civil servant, the sukkal (𒈛 (sukkal)).
x: As Inanna prepares to descend she fastens the seven divine laws to her side, and as she walks toward the netherworld she speaks to her vizier, Ninshubur.
Momus is not otherwise attested as Zeus’s advisor, but in name and function he matches Apsu’s vizier Mummu.

g: A vicegerent, viceroy.
A fairy chess piece that can only be moved one space up, down, left or right.
